title: ResNet & Deep Architectures
blurb: Tests why deep plain networks degrade, how residual connections fix gradient flow and make identity easy, the ResNet family, Inception and EfficientNet, feature extraction against fine-tuning against training from scratch, and what the measurements showed.

refLinks.label: §69.2.2 Other Answers to “How Do We Scale CNNs Well”
§69.2.3 Transfer Learning: Feature Extraction vs. Fine-Tuning

questions.prompt: Why do gradients vanish in a very deep plain network?
options: Each layer adds a constant to the gradient, which cancels out.
The loss becomes zero after the first few epochs.
Deep networks have no activation functions.
Many factors below 1 multiply toward zero.
questions.explanation: Twenty or fifty factors below 1 multiply to almost nothing, so early layers barely update however much data there is.

questions.prompt: If each of 20 layers scales the gradient by 0.8, what fraction of the gradient reaches the first layer? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: 0.8^20 = 0.0115, about 1% of the signal. Fifty such layers would leave 0.8^50 ≈ 0.000014.

questions.prompt: What does a residual block output?
options: F(x) × x, the residual times the input
F(x) + x, the learned residual plus the input
H(x), learned directly with no shortcut
x alone, with F(x) used only during training
questions.explanation: The block learns F(x) = H(x) − x and adds x back. The identity path gives gradients a direct route.

questions.prompt: Why can't the gradient through F(x) + x vanish to exactly zero just from stacking blocks?
options: Residual blocks have no weights to update.
The identity path adds +1 to the derivative.
The learning rate grows with network depth.
Batch normalisation rescales every gradient to 1.
questions.explanation: d(F(x) + x)/dx = F′(x) + 1. The +1 gives an additive path around the multiplicative chain.

questions.prompt: Why is "do nothing" easy for a residual block?
options: The skip connection disables the block after training.
Batch normalisation sets each output to zero.
Residual blocks start with all weights frozen.
F(x) near zero passes the input through.
questions.explanation: An unneeded block can learn to approximate identity, so extra depth doesn't have to hurt.

options: Using batch normalisation inside the residual block
Applying ReLU after the addition
Using 3×3 kernels in both convolutions
Adding mismatched shapes without a 1×1 projection
questions.explanation: Mismatched shapes can't be added. A 1×1 convolution on the shortcut fixes them. The other three match Listing 69.1.

questions.prompt: What is the bottleneck block in ResNet-50 and deeper?
options: 1×1 to shrink, 3×3, then 1×1 to restore
A 7×7 convolution followed by max-pooling
Parallel convolutions of several sizes, concatenated
Two 3×3 convolutions with a skip connection
questions.explanation: It is cheaper per layer, which allows more depth at similar compute. ResNet-18 and 34 use the two-conv block.

options: How to run several kernel sizes in one block
How to transfer ImageNet features to new domains
How to make very deep networks trainable at all
How to split compute across depth, width and resolution
questions.explanation: Compound scaling grows all three together. Trainability is ResNet's question, and parallel kernels are Inception's.

questions.prompt: In feature extraction, what gets trained?
options: The whole network at a small learning rate
The backbone only, with the head frozen
Nothing. The pretrained model is used as is.
Only a new final layer, with the backbone frozen
questions.explanation: Listing 69.3 sets requires_grad = False on the backbone and trains only the new fc head. It is cheap and hard to overfit.

refLinks.label: §69.2.3 Transfer Learning: Feature Extraction vs. Fine-Tuning

questions.prompt: Why is fine-tuning done at a much smaller learning rate than the new head?
options: So noisy steps don't wreck pretrained features
Because the head needs more epochs than the backbone
Because pretrained layers can't change at large rates
So training finishes faster
questions.explanation: The pretrained features are valuable. Large updates on a small target set can wipe them out.

refLinks.label: §69.2.3 Transfer Learning: Feature Extraction vs. Fine-Tuning

questions.prompt: Per Procedure 69.2, what should you do with a very different domain, such as satellite or synthetic images?
options: Skip validation, since pretrained models always transfer.
Always use feature extraction, since it can't overfit.
Test all three approaches on a held-out set.
Always fine-tune the whole network, since more capacity helps.
questions.explanation: For a different domain the guide says test, don't assume. The worked example showed why.

questions.prompt: At epoch 10, the residual network had 0.998 train accuracy and the plain one 0.687. What was the only difference between them?
options: The training data
The number of parameters
The depth of the network
The skip connections
questions.explanation: Depth, width, parameter count and training were identical. The residual network converged far faster.

questions.prompt: Final test accuracy was 0.989 for the residual network and 0.958 for the plain one. How many percentage points apart are they? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 0.989 − 0.958 = 0.031, or 3.1 points, with identical size and training budget.

questions.prompt: In the transfer experiment, which approach won?
options: All three tied within noise
Fine-tuning the pretrained ResNet, at 0.561
Training a small CNN from scratch, at 0.842
Feature extraction on the frozen backbone, at 0.633
questions.explanation: The from-scratch model had fewer parameters than the feature-extraction head alone and still won outright.

questions.prompt: Why did fine-tuning do worse than feature extraction here?
options: The learning rate was too small to change anything.
Fine-tuning froze more layers than feature extraction.
8.4 million parameters overfit the small dataset.
The pretrained weights were loaded incorrectly.
questions.explanation: Unfreezing more capacity became a liability with little target data. That is the trade-offs section's warning measured.

questions.prompt: Fine-tuning trained 8,398,858 parameters and the from-scratch model 3,658. About how many times more is that? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: 8,398,858 / 3,658 = 2,296, "over 2,000x". The far smaller model won on this different, data-poor domain.

bookExercises.prompt: Write the residual block's function ($F(x) + x$ instead of $H(x)$ directly) and explain in one sentence why the $+x$ term prevents the gradient from vanishing to exactly zero.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `F(x) + x` instead of `H(x)` directly. Because the derivative of `F(x) + x` with respect to `x` always includes a `+1` term (from differentiating the identity `x` path), the total gradient can never be driven to exactly zero purely by the multiplicative chain through `F`, unlike a plain block where the gradient is a pure product of per-layer terms that can shrink toward zero.

bookExercises.prompt: State Procedure 69.2's two questions for deciding between feature extraction, fine-tuning, and from-scratch.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: (1) How similar is the target domain to the pretrained model's training domain? (2) How much target training data is available?

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's plain-vs-residual table (epoch 10: plain 0.687, residual 0.998), explain what this early-epoch gap suggests about where in training the vanishing-gradient problem does most of its damage, given that both networks have identical size and training budget.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The dramatic epoch-10 gap (plain 0.687 vs. residual 0.998, with both networks identical in size and training budget) suggests vanishing gradients do most of their damage early in training, when weights are still far from a good solution and need large, informative gradient updates to move efficiently. The plain network's early layers are receiving a severely attenuated signal at exactly the point where a strong signal matters most for making rapid initial progress. The plain network does eventually make substantial progress (0.981 by epoch 60), suggesting some gradient signal does get through over many epochs, just far less efficiently than the residual network's direct path provides from the start.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's transfer-learning table (feature extraction 0.633, fine-tuning 0.561, from-scratch 0.842, with trainable parameters 5,130 / 8,398,858 / 3,658 respectively), explain specifically why MORE trainable parameters (fine-tuning) produced WORSE accuracy than feature extraction here, connecting your answer to the target dataset's size.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Fine-tuning's larger trainable-parameter count (8,398,858, versus feature extraction's 5,130) becomes a liability rather than an advantage specifically because the target dataset is small relative to that capacity. With only a limited number of target examples, a network with millions of trainable parameters has enough freedom to fit noise and idiosyncrasies in the small training set rather than learning genuinely generalizable patterns, producing worse held-out test accuracy despite (or because of) its larger capacity. Feature extraction's much smaller trainable-parameter count (only the new head) is far less prone to this overfitting, which is why it outperforms fine-tuning here even though fine-tuning nominally has "more information" (unfrozen backbone weights) available to adapt.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague says "always start with a pretrained ImageNet backbone and fine-tune it, training from scratch is basically never worth trying." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say in response.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "This chapter's own Worked Example measured the opposite on a domain visually different from ImageNet: a from-scratch model with only 3,658 parameters, fewer than the feature-extraction head alone, reached 0.842 test accuracy, beating both feature extraction (0.633) and fine-tuning (0.561). Pretrained features only help to the extent they're relevant to the target domain, and fine-tuning's larger capacity is actively risky on small target datasets. The right move is testing all three approaches on your specific task, not defaulting to fine-tuning as a rule."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 69.1 warns about shape mismatches when adding a residual connection. Describe a concrete architectural change (e.g. changing channel count between blocks) that would require the projection-shortcut variant rather than the plain identity shortcut, and explain why.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: If a residual stage doubles the channel count between blocks (a common pattern in deeper ResNet variants, e.g. going from 64 to 128 channels between stages), the identity shortcut `x` has 64 channels while the block's output `F(x)` has 128 channels. These shapes cannot be added directly. The projection-shortcut variant is required here: a 1x1 convolution on the shortcut path maps the 64-channel input to 128 channels (and can also apply a matching stride if the block also downsamples spatially), so the shapes align for the final addition.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about EfficientNet's compound scaling (Tan & Le, 2019). Explain in your own words why scaling depth, width, and resolution together in a fixed ratio outperforms scaling just one of these axes at the same total compute cost.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Scaling only one axis (e.g. depth alone) tends to hit diminishing returns because a network that's very deep but proportionally narrow, or high-resolution but shallow, wastes some of its added compute on a dimension that isn't the actual bottleneck for that architecture. A very deep but narrow network may lack the channel capacity to represent enough distinct features per layer, regardless of how many layers it has. Compound scaling increases depth, width, and resolution together in a balanced ratio because a network processing higher-resolution input genuinely benefits from more layers (to grow the receptive field enough to cover the larger image) and more channels (to capture the finer-grained detail the higher resolution provides) simultaneously. Scaling all three in a fixed, empirically-tuned ratio avoids compute being spent on one axis while another remains the limiting factor.
